t: Life insurance business in India was nationalised in 1956, while general insurance business was nationalised with effect from:
o: 1 January 1973
19 April 2000
1 September 1956
1 April 1971
e: The General Insurance Business (Nationalisation) Act, 1972 came into force on 1 January 1973, merging 107 insurers into four subsidiaries of GIC. LIC was formed in September 1956.

t: 'Insurance penetration' as used in industry statistics is measured as:
o: Total premium as a percentage of GDP
Premium per head of population
Number of policies per thousand people
Claims paid as a percentage of premium
e: Penetration is premium divided by GDP; 'density' is premium per capita. India's overall penetration has hovered around 4% of GDP, well below the global average, which is a core reason for the 'Insurance for All by 2047' vision.

t: The 'fraud diamond' model extends Cressey's fraud triangle by adding which fourth element?
o: Capability
Corruption
Concealment
Collusion
e: Wolfe and Hermanson added 'capability' — the personal traits and position that allow a person to actually execute the fraud — to pressure, opportunity and rationalisation.

t: 'Premium diversion' as a category of insurance fraud refers to:
o: Refund of premium on cancellation
Embezzlement of premiums collected from policyholders by agents or insurers instead of remitting or applying them to the policy
Charging a lower premium to selected customers
Transfer of premium between two policies of the same insured
e: Premium diversion is the most common type of intermediary/insider fraud worldwide: premiums are collected but pocketed, leaving the customer uninsured. It is distinct from legitimate transfers or refunds.

t: Studies in several markets suggest that fraudulent claims account for roughly what proportion of general insurance claim costs?
o: Around 40%
More than 60%
Around 10% (estimates range between 5% and 15%)
Less than 1%
e: Industry estimates in Europe, the USA and India generally place fraud at about 5–15% of claims costs, with 10% often cited as a working figure. This leakage is ultimately borne by honest policyholders through higher premiums.

t: A claims manager notices that a particular garage's invoices are always exactly 10% below the surveyor's assessment and contain identical part descriptions across unrelated vehicles. This observation is best described as:
o: Evidence of underinsurance
Proof of fraud sufficient for prosecution
Red flags warranting investigation of possible collusion between the garage and the surveyor
Normal commercial practice requiring no action
e: Red flags are indicators, not proof; they justify investigation. Consistent patterning between a repairer and an assessor suggests collusion, which must be established through verification before any repudiation or criminal complaint.

t: The National Insurance Crime Bureau (NICB) is a not-for-profit organisation that combats insurance fraud and vehicle theft in:
o: United Kingdom
United States of America
Singapore
South Africa
e: NICB, formed in 1992 from the merger of two earlier bodies, partners with US insurers and law enforcement, maintaining databases on vehicle theft and questionable claims.

t: In the UK, the Insurance Fraud Enforcement Department (IFED) is a specialist police unit funded by the insurance industry and housed within the:
o: Metropolitan Police
City of London Police
Financial Conduct Authority
Serious Fraud Office
e: IFED, launched in 2012 within the City of London Police, investigates and prosecutes insurance fraud referred by insurers through the Insurance Fraud Bureau.

t: The Association of Certified Fraud Examiners (ACFE) classifies occupational fraud into three primary categories. These are:
o: Claims fraud, underwriting fraud and investment fraud
Internal, external and collusive fraud
Hard fraud, soft fraud and cyber fraud
Asset misappropriation, corruption and financial statement fraud
e: ACFE's fraud tree groups occupational fraud into asset misappropriation (most frequent), corruption and financial statement fraud (least frequent but costliest). Insurers use this taxonomy when designing internal controls.

t: The foreign direct investment limit in Indian insurance companies was raised to 74% in which year?
e: ★ Key fact (repeated across the mocks of this paper). The Insurance (Amendment) Act, 2021 raised the FDI cap from 49% (set in 2015) to 74%. The original 2000 opening permitted 26%.

t: IRDAI's fraud monitoring framework requires insurers to report fraud statistics to the Authority:
o: Only on specific demand by the Authority
Every day through the Bima Sugam portal
Only when the fraud exceeds ₹1 crore
Annually, within the prescribed period after the close of the financial year
e: Insurers must file annual fraud monitoring returns in the formats prescribed, in addition to periodic internal reporting to their boards. There is no monetary threshold for reporting.

t: Under Section 41 of the Insurance Act, 1938, offering a rebate of commission or premium as an inducement to take out a policy is prohibited. The penalty for contravention after the 2015 amendment can extend to:
o: ₹25 lakh
₹1 crore
₹10 lakh
e: The Insurance Laws (Amendment) Act, 2015 raised the penalty under Section 41 from ₹500 to up to ₹10 lakh. Rebating distorts fair competition and is often linked to mis-selling and churning.

t: Which of the following is NOT one of the functions expected of an insurer's Fraud Monitoring Unit under the IRDAI framework?
o: Creating fraud awareness among employees and intermediaries
Monitoring and investigating suspected fraud cases
Fixing the sum insured for each policy issued
Co-ordinating with law enforcement agencies on fraud cases
e: The FMU monitors, investigates, builds awareness and liaises with police and other insurers; sum insured determination is an underwriting function, not a fraud-monitoring task.

t: A life insurer repudiates a claim within three years of policy issue citing fraud, but sends the nominee only a one-line letter stating 'claim rejected for fraud'. Which Section 45 requirement has the insurer failed to meet?
o: The requirement to wait for five years before repudiating
The requirement to communicate in writing the grounds and materials on which the decision is based
The requirement to obtain IRDAI's prior approval
The requirement to pay the full sum assured first
e: Section 45 obliges the insurer to communicate in writing to the insured or nominee the grounds and materials on which repudiation is based. A bare rejection without reasons is not compliant.

t: A fire claim is lodged for a godown that was insured for ₹80 lakh. Investigation finds that the insured's bank had initiated recovery proceedings two weeks before the fire and that CCTV cameras were switched off the previous evening. These facts primarily indicate:
o: A legitimate claim because the godown was insured
Inadequate fire-fighting arrangements
Underinsurance
Financial motive and opportunity consistent with a suspected arson-for-profit
e: Financial distress (motive) combined with disabling of surveillance (opportunity/concealment) are classic arson indicators. The insurer should commission a forensic fire investigation before deciding the claim.

t: Forensic fire investigators look for the 'point of origin' and burn patterns. A fire with a low burn at floor level spreading in an irregular 'pour' pattern most strongly suggests:
o: Lightning
Electrical short circuit
Use of a liquid accelerant
Spontaneous combustion of stock
e: Irregular pour or trail patterns on the floor indicate a flammable liquid was spread, pointing to arson. Electrical fires usually originate at wiring or appliances and spontaneous combustion starts inside a mass of material.

t: Under Section 164 of the Motor Vehicles Act, 1988 (as amended in 2019), the compensation payable on a 'no fault' basis in case of death caused by a motor vehicle accident is:
e: ★ Key fact (repeated across the mocks of this paper). Section 164 fixes no-fault compensation at ₹5 lakh for death and ₹2.5 lakh for grievous hurt. Fraudsters sometimes fabricate accident records to claim these amounts from insurers.

t: Advance Loss of Profits (ALOP) / Delay in Start-Up cover under project insurance is exposed to fraud mainly through:
o: Attributing delays caused by the contractor's own financing or planning failures to an insured physical damage event
Claiming for damage caused by earthquake
Claiming debris removal costs
Reporting damage to third-party property
e: ALOP pays only for delay that results from insured material damage. Fraudulent claims try to link delays actually caused by funding gaps, approvals or poor planning to a minor insured event.

t: 'Barratry' in marine insurance means:
o: Voluntary sacrifice of cargo to save the ship
A wrongful act wilfully committed by the master or crew to the prejudice of the shipowner
Deviation from the agreed route for repairs
Deliberate sinking of a ship by its owner
e: Barratry is fraud or wrongful conduct by master or crew against the owner's interest (for example, selling cargo and scuttling). It is covered under hull clauses only if the owner is not privy to it.

t: A cargo claim is supported by a bill of lading, invoice and packing list, but the shipping line confirms that the vessel named never called at the load port on the stated date. This is an instance of:
o: General average
Constructive total loss
Short landing due to pilferage
Documentary fraud / non-shipment of cargo
e: Non-shipment frauds use forged shipping documents for cargo that was never loaded. Verification with the carrier, port records and vessel tracking exposes such claims.

t: Why do fraudsters often over-insure cargo (for example, insuring at 150% of its true value) under a marine cargo policy?
o: Because it is mandatory under the Marine Insurance Act
Because a deliberate loss then yields a profit over the real value of the goods
Because customs duty is refunded on insured value
Because premium rates fall at higher sums insured
e: Over-insurance creates a profit motive for intentional loss or diversion of cargo. Usual practice is to insure at CIF plus a 10% margin; a much higher value is a red flag at underwriting.

t: Under a Money Insurance (cash-in-transit) policy, which of the following claim scenarios is a classic fraud pattern?
o: Loss of cash by the carrying employee due to an actual road accident
Theft of cash from a locked safe by burglars using explosives
Loss of cash in a fire at the insured's office safe
An employee reports a staged robbery of cash en route to the bank after having already misappropriated the money
e: Fictitious hold-ups reported by the carrying employee are the most common money-in-transit fraud, often to cover prior embezzlement. The other scenarios are genuine insured events.

t: In a fidelity guarantee policy, the 'discovery period' is significant because:
o: Losses must be discovered within that period after the employee leaves or the policy ends to be covered
It fixes the period within which the employee must repay the money
It is the time allowed to the insurer to settle the claim
It defines how long the employer must employ the person
e: Fidelity policies cover losses committed during the policy period but discovered within a specified period (typically 12 months) after termination of employment or expiry of cover. Late discoveries beyond this are excluded.

t: Overseas travel insurance is vulnerable to which of the following frauds?
o: Fabricated or inflated medical bills from foreign hospitals and false baggage-loss claims
Loss arising from flight cancellation due to weather
Claims for pre-booked hotel costs
Claims for passport replacement fees
e: Fake or inflated overseas medical invoices and fictitious lost-baggage claims (often with forged airline property irregularity reports) are prominent travel insurance frauds. The other items are ordinary insured events.

t: A 'paper accident' in motor third-party fraud is one where:
o: The accident was recorded only on paper by the police
The claimant has no written policy document
The insurer settles the claim without a survey
No accident actually occurred; the FIR, injury records and witness statements are fabricated to file a claim before the Motor Accident Claims Tribunal
e: Paper accidents involve fabricated police and hospital records, often with collusion among touts, doctors and advocates, to claim compensation from insurers. Verification of hospital registers and police diaries is key.

t: Which of the following databases most directly helps an Indian insurer detect that the same vehicle has been insured with multiple insurers or has earlier claims?
o: IIB motor insurance database and the VAHAN registry
Income tax e-filing portal
GST network
Passport Seva portal
e: The IIB repository and the Ministry of Road Transport's VAHAN data allow cross-checking of vehicle, ownership, policy and claim history across insurers, exposing duplicate cover and repeat claimants.

t: A car with an IDV of ₹6 lakh is reported stolen. During investigation, the insured's phone records place him at a dealership 200 km away on the night of the 'theft', and the vehicle is later found registered in another state under a changed engine number. The most probable scheme is:
o: Genuine theft with subsequent re-registration by a thief
Hit-and-run
Total loss due to accident
Sale of the vehicle followed by a false theft claim
e: Selling the vehicle (often across state lines) and then reporting it stolen to recover the IDV is a well-known 'fake theft' fraud. Phone location data and RTO records are standard investigative tools.

t: Under motor insurance, which of the following is a fraud risk indicator relating to the driver rather than the vehicle?
o: Vehicle has a factory-fitted anti-theft device
Driving licence submitted is found to be fake or issued for a different class of vehicle
Claim is for a third-party property damage
Vehicle is less than one year old
e: Fake or non-matching driving licences are a frequent fraud, since a valid licence of the correct class is a policy condition. The other options are neutral facts.

t: Under the Employees' Compensation Act, 1923, the minimum compensation payable in case of death of an employee arising out of and in the course of employment is:
e: ★ Key fact (repeated across the mocks of this paper). Compensation for death is 50% of monthly wages multiplied by the relevant age factor, subject to a minimum of ₹1,20,000. Permanent total disablement carries a minimum of ₹1,40,000.

t: 'Upcoding' in health insurance fraud is:
o: Charging for a longer stay than permitted
Using a wrong policy number
Billing for a more complex or expensive procedure or diagnosis than the one actually performed
Billing for services never rendered
e: Upcoding manipulates procedure/diagnosis codes to attract a higher package rate. Phantom billing is charging for non-existent services and unbundling is splitting a procedure into separately billed components.

t: The Registry of Hospitals in Network of Insurance (ROHINI), maintained by IIB, helps control health fraud by:
o: Issuing licences to hospitals
Processing cashless authorisations
Fixing package rates for all hospitals
Providing a unique identifier for each hospital so that bills from fake or de-listed hospitals can be detected
e: ROHINI assigns a unique ID to every hospital in insurers'/TPAs' networks, enabling verification of hospital existence, standardised data and tracking of suspicious providers across the industry.

t: A reimbursement health claim shows a seven-day hospitalisation for 'fever', but the discharge summary records no investigations, no IV medication and vital signs within normal limits throughout. The most appropriate conclusion is:
o: The claim should be paid as the hospital is in the network
Hospitalisation appears medically unnecessary and the claim should be investigated for possible fabricated admission
Only the room rent should be deducted
The claim is payable as hospitalisation exceeded 24 hours
e: Admission without active line of treatment for a condition manageable on an out-patient basis is a recognised red flag for fraudulent or unnecessary hospitalisation, frequently arranged in collusion with the hospital.

t: Which of the following is NOT a provider-side (hospital) health insurance fraud?
o: Admitting patients for unnecessary procedures to utilise the sum insured
A patient concealing a pre-existing disease in the proposal form
Billing branded drugs while dispensing generics
Unbundling a surgical package into separate bills
e: Concealment of pre-existing disease is a policyholder (application) fraud. Unbundling, substitution of drugs and unnecessary admissions are all committed by providers.

t: Product liability claims are vulnerable to fraud when:
o: A manufacturer recalls a defective batch voluntarily
A court awards compensation on proved negligence
A claimant deliberately damages a product or plants a foreign object and alleges it caused injury
The insured notifies a genuine injury promptly
e: Planted contaminants (for example in packaged food) and self-inflicted damage are classic product liability frauds. Insurers rely on laboratory tests, batch records and timing analysis to expose them.

t: Under the Employees' Compensation Act, 1923, compensation for death is computed as 50% of monthly wages multiplied by the relevant age factor. If a 30-year-old employee (factor 207.98) earning ₹15,000 per month dies in a work accident, the compensation is approximately:
e: 50% × ₹15,000 = ₹7,500; ₹7,500 × 207.98 = ₹15,59,850. Fraud in EC claims often involves inflating the declared wage or understating the employee's age to increase the factor.

t: Under IRDAI's 2024 norms, a surveyor must be appointed within what time of a claim intimation?
o: 24 hours
48 hours
72 hours
7 days
e: ★ Core fact (asked across III papers). Appointment within 24 hours; survey report within 15 days; insurer's decision within 7 days of the report.

t: Professional Indemnity insurance for doctors is exposed to fraud primarily through:
o: Collusive or exaggerated negligence claims where the patient and a third party inflate damages or fabricate the alleged error
Claims for damage to the doctor's clinic from fire
Claims for the doctor's own illness
Claims for loss of professional licence
e: PI cover responds to legal liability for professional negligence; fraud arises from fabricated or exaggerated allegations and collusion. The other items are not within PI scope.

t: Which of the following is a common fraud in poultry insurance?
o: Allowing the insurer's veterinarian to inspect the farm
Inflating the number of birds that died from disease and claiming for birds that were actually sold
Vaccinating birds as per schedule
Maintaining daily mortality records
e: Overstatement of mortality, sale of healthy birds reported as dead and manipulated mortality registers are typical poultry claim frauds. The other options are good practices that reduce fraud risk.

t: Under PMFBY, yield loss at the end of the season is assessed on an 'area approach' using:
o: Satellite imagery alone
Each farmer's self-declaration of harvest
Crop Cutting Experiments (CCEs) conducted in the notified insurance unit
The previous year's yield
e: PMFBY compares actual yield from CCEs in the insurance unit with the threshold yield. Fraud risks include manipulation of CCE results and misreporting of sown area, which technology (smartphone-based CCE capture, remote sensing) seeks to curb.

t: A farmer insures five buffaloes; one dies and a claim is paid. Six months later, another claim is received with the same ear-tag number for a different buffalo. The appropriate inference is:
o: Genuine claim since the farmer owns several animals
Tag re-use / recycling fraud, requiring rejection and investigation
Clerical error by the insurer; pay the claim
The second animal was automatically insured
e: Each tag is unique to one insured animal and is surrendered on claim; its reappearance indicates it was removed and reattached to another animal. This is a well-documented livestock fraud.

t: A death claim is lodged on a policy taken eight months earlier for a sum assured of ₹1 crore, where the proposer's declared annual income was ₹3 lakh and no medical examination was required. The claim should be treated as:
o: A claim to be referred to the Ombudsman
An early claim with financial and medical red flags, warranting investigation
A routine claim to be settled within 30 days without enquiry
A claim to be rejected outright under Section 45
e: A sum assured grossly disproportionate to income, early death and non-medical underwriting are classic red flags. Investigation (hospital records, income proof, cause of death) must precede any decision; outright rejection without enquiry would violate Section 45 and policyholder protection norms.

t: 'Churning' by a life insurance agent means:
o: Inducing a policyholder to surrender an existing policy and buy a new one mainly to earn fresh commission
Selling multiple policies to the same family
Collecting renewal premium in cash
Transferring the policy to a new agent
e: Churning (or twisting) is a mis-selling practice that harms the customer through surrender losses and fresh acquisition charges while enriching the agent; it is a form of intermediary fraud.

t: Which of the following is a fraud involving a person who is already dead or terminally ill?
o: Taking a policy in the name of a terminally ill person with a healthy impersonator at the medical examination, to claim on early death
Reviving a lapsed policy with a declaration of good health that is true
Taking a term policy at age 30 with full disclosure
Assigning a policy to a bank for a loan
e: Insuring persons already dead or near death, using impersonation and forged documents, is among the most serious life frauds, often involving agents. The other options are legitimate transactions.

t: Under Section 45 of the Insurance Act, 1938, 'mere silence' as to facts likely to affect the risk is:
o: Always fraud
Fraud only in unit-linked policies
Not fraud, unless the circumstances show it was the duty of the insured to speak or silence is itself equivalent to speaking
Fraud only if the agent was aware
e: Section 45 adopts the Contract Act position that silence is not fraud unless there is a duty to disclose or silence is equivalent to speech. The proposal form questions create such a duty for the matters asked.

t: An investigator interviewing a claimant should:
o: Threaten the claimant with police action to obtain admissions
Offer part payment in exchange for a withdrawal
Rely only on telephone conversations without any record
Record the statement in the claimant's own words, have it signed and dated, and avoid leading questions
e: Statements must be voluntary, accurately recorded and signed to be credible evidence. Coercion or inducement destroys the evidentiary value and exposes the insurer to legal and regulatory action.

t: For health insurance, the maximum time an insurer may take to decide a cashless authorisation request under the 2024 master circular is:
o: 1 hour
3 hours
6 hours
24 hours
e: ★ Core fact (asked across III papers). Cashless authorisation within 1 hour of request; final discharge authorisation within 3 hours.

t: Under the IRDAI regulations on protection of policyholders' interests, where a general insurance claim requires investigation, the insurer should complete the investigation and settle the claim within:
o: Investigation within 90 days and settlement within 180 days
Investigation within 7 days and settlement within 15 days
No time limit applies when investigation is needed
Investigation within 30 days of receipt of the last necessary document and settlement within 45 days
e: The policyholder protection framework requires investigation to be completed within 30 days and the claim to be settled within 45 days of the last document, with interest payable for delay. Investigation cannot be used as an excuse for indefinite delay.

t: Which of the following is an example of 'open-source intelligence' (OSINT) in claim investigation?
o: Checking the claimant's public social media posts showing physical activity during the alleged disability period
Obtaining the claimant's bank statements without consent
Intercepting the claimant's phone calls
Hacking into the hospital's records
e: OSINT uses publicly available information such as social media, company filings and news. Interception, unauthorised data access and hacking are illegal and inadmissible.

t: Under the Prevention of Money Laundering Act, 2002, the punishment for the offence of money laundering is rigorous imprisonment for:
o: Not less than 10 years
Fine only, without imprisonment
Not less than 3 years, extendable to 7 years, with fine
Not less than 1 year, extendable to 3 years
e: Section 4 of PMLA prescribes rigorous imprisonment of 3 to 7 years and fine (up to 10 years where the offence relates to specified narcotics offences).

t: Which of the following life insurance transactions is the strongest money-laundering red flag?
o: Purchase of a large single-premium policy with cash followed by surrender within the free-look period and a request to refund to a third-party account
Nomination changed in favour of the spouse
Policy loan taken after five years of regular premium payment
Monthly premium of ₹2,000 paid through ECS on a term policy
e: Large cash single premiums, early surrender/free-look cancellation and refund to unrelated accounts are textbook laundering techniques (placement and layering). The other transactions are ordinary.
